title: The Story of Sir Pellias: Chapter 6
paragraphs: _How the Lady of the Lake Took Back Her Necklace From Sir Pellias._

When the next morning came, Sir Gawaine called his esquire to him and said, “Bring me my armor and help me put it on.” The esquire did so. Then Sir Gawaine said, “Help me onto my horse,” and the esquire did that as well. It was still very early. The grass was bright and sparkling with dew, and the little birds sang so loudly and gladly that anyone would have been glad to be alive. So once Sir Gawaine was in his armor and on horseback, he began to feel braver, and the dark clouds that had hung over him lifted a little. He spoke to his esquire in a stronger voice. “Take this glove of mine to Sir Pellias and tell him that Sir Gawaine is riding in the meadow in front of the castle, and that he challenges Sir Pellias to meet him there, on horseback or on foot, whichever that knight prefers.”

The esquire was very surprised. Sir Gawaine and Sir Pellias had always been such close friends that there were hardly any friends like them in all that land, and everyone spoke of their love for one another. But the esquire kept his thoughts to himself and only said, “Will you not eat something before you go to battle?” Sir Gawaine answered, “No, I will not eat until I have fought. Now go and do as I told you.”

So Sir Gawaine’s esquire went to Sir Pellias in his tent. He gave the knight Sir Gawaine’s glove and told him the message. Sir Pellias said, “Tell your master that I will come out to meet him as soon as I have eaten my breakfast.”

News of the challenge reached Sir Brandiles, Sir Mador de la Porte, Sir Ewaine and Sir Marhaus, and these knights were very troubled by it. Sir Ewaine said to the others, “Gentlemen, let us go and find out what this is about.” So the four knights went to the white tent where Sir Pellias was eating his breakfast.
When they stood before Sir Pellias, Sir Ewaine said to him, “What is this quarrel between my kinsman and you?” Sir Pellias answered, “I will not tell you. Leave it alone and do not meddle in it.”
Then Sir Ewaine said, “Would you really fight your friend in earnest?” Sir Pellias replied, “He is no friend of mine any longer.”

Then Sir Brandiles cried out, “It is a great pity that a quarrel should come between friends like you and Sir Gawaine. Will you not let us make peace between you?” But Sir Pellias answered, “You cannot make peace. This quarrel cannot be stopped until it has been fought to its end.”
Then the knights saw that their words were useless, and they left Sir Pellias and went away.

When Sir Pellias had finished his breakfast, he called an esquire named Montenoir and ordered him to help him put on the red armor that he had worn all this time. Montenoir did so. Then, dressed in that armor, Sir Pellias rode out into the meadow before the castle, where Sir Gawaine was riding up and down. The four other knights came to him once more and begged him to make peace with Sir Gawaine. But Sir Pellias would not listen to them, so they left him again, and he rode out into the field before the castle of Grantmesnle.

By now a great crowd of people had gathered on the castle walls to watch the combat, for the news had spread all around the place. People had also learned that the knight who would fight Sir Pellias was the famous royal knight Sir Gawaine, the son of King Lot of Orkney and a nephew of King Arthur. So everyone was eager to see such a famous knight in battle.

The Lady Ettard also came down to the walls and stood in a smaller tower that looked over the field. From there she saw that Sir Pellias wore the necklace of emeralds, opals and gold over his armor. Her heart went out to him because of it, and she hoped that he would win.

Then each knight took his place where he thought best. They set their spears and shields and made themselves ready. When they were fully prepared, Sir Marhaus gave the signal to begin. At once each knight left his place and charged at the other as fast as lightning, so fiercely that the ground thundered and shook under their horses’ hooves. They met squarely in the middle of the field, each striking the other right in the center of his shield. In that clash the spear of Sir Gawaine broke all the way to the hand-guard, but the spear of Sir Pellias held firm. Sir Gawaine was thrown from his saddle with terrible force. He hit the ground so hard that he rolled three times in the dust, and then he lay completely still, as though he were dead.
At this, all the people on the walls shouted aloud, for it was a truly splendid combat.

Then the four knights who had been watching hurried to Sir Gawaine where he lay, while Sir Pellias rode back and waited on his horse close by. Sir Ewaine and Sir Gawaine’s esquire quickly unlaced Sir Gawaine’s helmet. And, look! His face was the color of ashes, and they could not see that he was breathing.

Then Sir Marhaus said, “I believe you have killed this knight, Sir Pellias.” Sir Pellias said, “Do you think so?” “Yes,” said Sir Marhaus, “and I think it a great pity.” Sir Pellias answered, “He has not suffered more than he deserved.”

At these words Sir Ewaine was filled with anger and cried out, “Sir Knight, I think you forget who this knight is. He is not only a fellow companion of the Round Table, to whom you have sworn complete brotherhood. He is also the son of a king and the nephew of King Arthur himself.”
But Sir Pellias kept a very steady face and answered, “I would not be sorry for this even if that knight were a king in his own right instead of the son of a king.”
Then Sir Ewaine raised his voice in great anger and shouted at Sir Pellias, “Go away, or something terrible will happen to you!” “Very well,” said Sir Pellias, “I will go.”
With that he turned his horse and rode away. He entered the woods and was soon out of their sight.

Then the others lifted up Sir Gawaine and carried him to the tent that had lately been Sir Pellias’s, and they laid him on Sir Pellias’s bed. It was more than an hour before he came to himself again, and for much of that time those beside him believed that he was dead.

But none of those knights knew the truth. Sir Pellias had been so badly wounded in the side in that fight that there was no hope he would live beyond that day. Although Sir Gawaine’s spear had broken, and Sir Pellias had thrown him down completely, the head of Sir Gawaine’s spear had pierced Sir Pellias’s armor. It had gone into his side and broken off there, so that a piece of iron as long as the breadth of a palm was left inside his body, a little above the waist. So, while Sir Pellias sat talking so firmly to those four knights, he was in terrible pain, and blood was running down inside his armor in great amounts. Because of the blood he had lost and the great agony he suffered, his head swam and felt as light as a feather the whole time he talked with them. But he said not a word to them about the terrible wound he had received. Instead he rode away proudly into the forest.
But once he was in the forest, he could hold back no longer. He began to groan bitterly and cried out, “Alas! Alas! I have surely received my death-wound in this battle!”

That morning the damsel Parcenet had ridden out to fly a young falcon, and a dwarf who belonged to the Lady Ettard had ridden with her for company. They were riding along the edge of the forest, not far from Grantmesnle, where the thick woods began and the thin woods ended. There the damsel heard a voice in the woods, crying out in great sorrow. She stopped and listened, and soon she heard the voice again, moaning loudly. Then Parcenet said to the dwarf, “What is that I hear? Surely it is someone crying in grief. Let us go and see who is making such a sad moan.” The dwarf said, “It shall be as you say.”

So the damsel and the dwarf went a little farther, and there they saw a knight sitting on a black horse beneath an oak tree. The knight was dressed completely in red armor, so Parcenet knew that it must be Sir Pellias. She saw that he was leaning the butt of his spear on the ground to hold himself up on his horse, for he would otherwise have fallen from weakness. And all the while he made the great moan that Parcenet had heard. Seeing him in such a sorry state, Parcenet was filled with pity and hurried to him, crying out, “Alas! Sir Pellias, what is wrong?”

Sir Pellias looked at her as though she were very far away. Because he was so faint, he saw her as if through thin water. He said very weakly, “Maiden, I am badly hurt.” She said, “How are you hurt, Sir Pellias?” He answered, “I have a terrible wound in my side. The point of a spear is still stuck there, about a palm’s breadth deep, so that it reaches almost to my heart. It seems to me that I will not live very long.”
At this the maiden cried out, “Alas! Alas! What is this!” She wept bitterly and wrung her hands in sorrow that such a noble knight should have come to such a terrible state.

Then the dwarf, seeing how deeply she was troubled by grief, said, “Damsel, I know of a place in this forest, though it is quite far from here, where a very holy hermit lives who is an exceptionally skilled healer. If we can bring this knight to the chapel where that hermit lives, I believe he may be helped back to health and comfort.”

Then Parcenet said, “Gansaret”—for Gansaret was the dwarf’s name—“Gansaret, let us take this knight there as quickly as we can. I tell you truly that I care for him very much.” “Very well,” said the dwarf, “I will show you where the chapel is.”

So the dwarf took the bridle of Sir Pellias’s horse and led the way through the forest, while Parcenet rode beside Sir Pellias and held him up in his saddle. From time to time Sir Pellias fainted from sickness and pain, and he would have fallen if she had not held him. So they went forward very sadly and so slowly that it was noon before they came to the thick and lonely part of the forest where the hermit lived.
When they reached that place, the dwarf said, “There, damsel, is the chapel I told you about.”

Then Parcenet lifted her eyes and saw a little chapel in the woods, built among the leafy trees. Around it was a small open lawn decked with flowers, and near the door of the hermitage was a fountain of water as clear as crystal. It was a hidden, lonely place, and very quiet and peaceful. In front of the chapel they saw a wild doe and her fawn grazing on the tender grass and herbs, without any fear of harm. When the dwarf, the maiden and the wounded knight came near, the doe and the fawn looked up with wide eyes and pricked up their large ears in wonder. But they did not run away, for they feared no harm, and soon they began to graze again. All around the chapel, in the branches of the trees, were great numbers of birds, singing and chirping cheerfully. The birds were waiting for the midday meal that the hermit used to throw to them.
(This was the same forest sanctuary where King Arthur had come when he was so badly wounded by Sir Pellinore, as was told earlier in this history.)

As the maiden, the dwarf and the wounded knight came near the chapel, a little bell began to ring very sweetly, and its sound echoed all through the quiet woods, for it was now the hour of noon. Sir Pellias heard the bell as though from far away. First he said, “Where have I come?” and then he managed to make the sign of the cross. Parcenet crossed herself, and the dwarf knelt down and crossed himself. When the bell stopped ringing, the dwarf cried out in a loud voice, “Hello! Hello! Here is someone who needs help!”

Then the door of the sanctuary opened, and a very old and respected man came out, with a long white beard like finely combed wool. And look! As he came out, all the birds that had been waiting flew around him in great numbers, for they thought he had come to feed them. So the hermit had to brush the little birds away with his hands as he walked over to the place where the three stood.

When he reached them, he asked who they were and why they had brought the wounded knight there. Parcenet told him how things stood with them, and how they had found Sir Pellias so badly wounded in the forest that morning and had brought him here.

When the hermit had heard her whole story, he said, “It is well, and I will take him in.” He took Sir Pellias into his cell, and when they had helped lay him on the bed, Parcenet and the dwarf went home again.

After they had gone, the hermit examined Sir Pellias’s wound, and Sir Pellias lay in a deep faint. The faint was so deep that the hermit saw it was the faint of death and that the knight was close to the end. He said, “This knight must surely die very soon, for I can do nothing to save him.” So he left Sir Pellias’s side at once and hurried to prepare the last sacrament, as is given to a noble knight who is dying.

While the hermit was busy with this, the door suddenly opened, and a very strange lady came into the room. She was dressed all in green, and around her arms she wore bracelets of emeralds and opals set in gold. Her hair was very soft and entirely black, and it was tied with a cord of crimson ribbon. The hermit saw that her face was as white as ivory and that her eyes shone like jewels set in ivory, and so he knew that she was no ordinary mortal.

The lady went straight to Sir Pellias and leaned over him so that her breath touched his forehead. She said, “Alas! Sir Pellias, that you should lie like this.” “Lady,” said the hermit, “you may well say ‘Alas,’ for this knight has only a few minutes left to live.” The lady answered, “Not so, holy man, for I tell you that this knight will live a long while yet.” When she had said this, she bent down and took from around his neck the necklace of emeralds, opals and gold that circled it, and she hung it around her own neck.
When the hermit saw what she did, he said, “Lady, what is this that you are doing, and why do you take that ornament from a dying man?”

But the lady answered very calmly, “I gave it to him, so I am only taking back what is mine. Now please let me stay with this knight for a little while, because I have great hope that I can bring him back to life.”
Then the hermit was doubtful and said, “Will you try to heal him by magic?” And the lady said, “If I do, it will not be black magic.”
So the hermit was satisfied. He went away and left the lady alone with Sir Pellias.

Once the lady was alone with the wounded knight, she began to do several very strange things. First she brought out a loadstone of great power and held it to the wound. And behold, the iron of the spear-head came out of the wound, and Sir Pellias groaned with great pain as it came. When the spear-point was out, blood burst from the wound like a crimson fountain. But the lady quickly pressed a fragrant napkin of fine linen against the wound and stopped the blood. It bled no more, for she held it inside the veins with powerful spells of magic. With the blood stopped, the lady took a small crystal bottle from her bosom. It was filled with a blue elixir that had a very unusual fragrance. She poured some of this elixir between the cold, gray lips of the knight. As soon as it touched his lips, life began to enter his body once more. In a little while he opened his eyes and looked about him with a very strange expression. The first thing he saw was the lady dressed in green standing beside him. She was so beautiful that he thought he might have died and gone to Paradise, so he said, “Am I dead, then?”

“No, you are not dead,” said the lady, “but you have been terribly close to death.” “Then where am I?” said Sir Pellias. She replied, “You are in a deep part of the forest, and this is the cell of a saintly hermit.” At this Sir Pellias said, “Who has brought me back to life?” The lady smiled and said, “I did.”

For a little while Sir Pellias lay very quiet. Then after a time he spoke and said, “Lady, I feel very strange.” “Yes,” said the lady, “that is because you now have a different life.” Then Sir Pellias said, “What has happened to me?” And the lady said, “This is how it is. To bring you back to life, I gave you a drink of an _elixir vitæ_. So now you are only half what you were before. By one half you are mortal, and by the other half you are fay.”

Then Sir Pellias looked up and saw that the lady wore around her neck the collar of emeralds, opals and gold that he had worn before. And behold, his heart went out to her with great warmth, and he said, “Lady, you say that I am half fay, and I can see that you are wholly fay. Now I beg you to let me stay near you from now on.” And the lady said, “It will be as you ask. That is the very reason I let you come close to death and then brought you back to life.”

Then Sir Pellias said, “When may I go with you?” And she said, “In a little while, when you have had something to drink.” “How can that be?” said Sir Pellias. “I am as weak as a little child.” The lady answered, “When you have drunk some water, your strength will return to you, and you will be completely well and whole again.”

So the Lady of the Lake went out and soon came back, carrying an earthen jug filled with water from the fountain close by. When Sir Pellias had drunk that water, he felt his strength suddenly come back to him entirely.

Yet he was not at all as he had been before. His body now felt as light as air, and his soul was filled with a pure joy such as he had never felt in his life. So he got up at once from his bed of pain and said, “You have given life to me again, and now I give that life to you forever.”

Then the lady looked at him and smiled with great kindness. She said, “Sir Pellias, I have thought tenderly of you ever since the day I saw you, in your young knighthood, drink a cup of milk at a cottager’s hut in this forest. The day was warm and you had set aside your helmet. A young milkmaid, brown-faced and barefoot, came and brought you a bowl of milk, and you drank it with great appetite. That was the first time I saw you, although you did not see me. Since then I have felt great friendship for all your fellowship at King Arthur’s Court, and for King Arthur himself, all for your sake.”

Then Sir Pellias said, “Lady, will you accept me as your knight?” and she said, “Yes.” Then Sir Pellias said, “May I kiss you?” And she said, “Yes, if it pleases you.” So Sir Pellias kissed her on the lips, and so they pledged themselves to each other.
Now let us return to Parcenet and the dwarf:

After those two had left the hermitage in the woodland, they made their way again toward Grantmesnle. When they had almost come out of the forest, at a place not far from the glade of trees where those fellow knights had made their camp, they met one of those knights in half-armor. That knight was Sir Mador de la Porte. Parcenet called to him by name and said, “Alas! Sir Mador, a short time ago I left a hermit’s cell in the forest, where I left Sir Pellias wounded almost to death. I fear he has only a little while to live.”
Then Sir Mador de la Porte cried out, “Ha! Maiden, what is this you tell me? That is very hard to believe, for when Sir Pellias left us this morning he showed no sign of any wound or sickness.”
But Parcenet replied, “All the same, I saw him myself, lying in great pain and sorrow. Before he fainted into the sleep of death, he told me himself that he had the iron of a spear in his side.”
Then Sir Mador de la Porte said, “Alas! Alas! That is sad news! Now, damsel, with your leave, I will go and hurry to my companions to tell them.” And Parcenet said, “Please do.”
So Sir Mador de la Porte hurried to the pavilion where his companions were, and he told them the news he had heard.

By this time Sir Gawaine had fully recovered from the violent fall he had suffered that morning. So when he heard the news that Sir Mador de la Porte brought, he struck his hands together and cried out loud, “Woe is me! What have I done! First I betrayed my friend, and now I have killed him. I will go out at once to find him and beg his forgiveness before he dies.”
But Sir Ewaine said, “What are you going to do? You are not yet fit to make any journey.”

Sir Gawaine said, “I do not care, for I am determined to go and find my friend.” He would not allow any of his companions to go with him. He called his esquire to bring his horse, mounted it, and rode away alone into the forest, heading west and mourning with great sorrow as he went.

Late in the afternoon, when the sun was sinking toward its setting and the light fell as red as fire through the forest leaves, Sir Gawaine came to the hermit’s cell, which stood in a silent and lonely part of the forest. He saw that the hermit was outside his cell, digging in a little garden of lentils. When the hermit saw the armed knight ride onto the lawn in the red light of the setting sun, he stopped digging and leaned on his trowel. Then Sir Gawaine came closer, and from his horse he told the holy man what business had brought him.

To this the hermit said, “A lady came here several hours ago. She was dressed all in green and looked very unusual, so it was easy to see that she was fay. By certain charms of magic that lady cured your friend, and after she had healed him, the two of them rode away into the forest together.”

Then Sir Gawaine was greatly amazed and said, “This is a very strange thing you tell me, that a dying knight should be brought back to life in so short a time, and should ride away so suddenly from his bed of pain. Now please tell me where they went.” The hermit said, “They went west.” When Sir Gawaine heard this, he said, “I will follow them.”

So he rode away and left the hermit gazing after him. As he rode on, twilight began to fall quickly, and soon the woods grew very dark and strange all around him. But as the darkness came down, a wonderful marvel happened. Behold, a pale blue light appeared in front of Sir Gawaine. It went ahead of him and showed him the way, and he followed it, full of wonder.

After he had followed the light for a very long time, he suddenly came to the place where the woods ended and a wide, open plain of great size began. The whole plain was lit by a strange glow like the light of a clear full moon, although no moon was shining at that time. In that pale, silver light Sir Gawaine could see everything with wonderful clearness. He saw that he was on a plain covered all over with flowers of many kinds. Their scent so filled the night that it seemed to press on his chest with a great pleasure. He saw that a great lake lay in front of him, very wide and still. All these things looked so strange in that light that Sir Gawaine knew he had come into a land of faëry. So he rode among the tall flowers toward the lake, half afraid, for he did not know what was going to happen to him.

As he drew near the lake, he saw a knight and a lady coming toward him. When they came close, he saw that the knight was Sir Pellias, and that his face looked exceedingly strange. He saw that the lady was the one he had seen before, dressed all in green, when he had traveled in the Forest of Adventure with Sir Ewaine and Sir Marhaus.

When Sir Gawaine first saw Sir Pellias, he was filled with great fear, for he thought he was looking at a spirit. But when he saw that Sir Pellias was alive, a joy as great as that fear came into his heart, and he hurried toward Sir Pellias. When he came near, he leaped from his horse, crying out, “Forgive me! Forgive me!” with great passion. Then he would have taken Sir Pellias in his arms, but Sir Pellias drew away from Sir Gawaine’s touch, though not in anger. Sir Pellias spoke in a voice that was thin and clear as silver, as though it came from far away. He said, “Do not touch me, for I am not as I was before. I am not all human, but part fay. As for my forgiveness, I forgive you whatever harm I may have suffered at your hands. And more than that, I give you my love, and I hope greatly for your joy and happiness. But now I am going away from you, dear friend, and perhaps I will not see you again. So I leave this with you as my last request: go back to King Arthur’s Court and make your peace with the Queen. Then you can bring them news of all that has happened to me.”
Then Sir Gawaine cried out in great sorrow, “Where are you going?”
And Sir Pellias said, “I am going to that wonderful city of gold and blue that lies in that valley of flowers.”
Then Sir Gawaine said, “I see no city, only a lake of water.”
Sir Pellias replied, “Even so, there is a city there, and I am going to it, so now I say farewell to you.”

Then Sir Gawaine looked into the face of Sir Pellias and saw again the strange light in it. It looked very unusual, for it was white like ivory, and his eyes shone like jewels set in ivory. A smile lay on his lips and never grew or faded but always stayed the same. (For those of that kind always looked this way and smiled in this manner. They were the Lady of the Lake, Sir Pellias, and Sir Launcelot of the Lake.)

Then Sir Pellias and the Lady of the Lake turned and left Sir Gawaine where he stood. They went toward the lake and entered it. When the feet of the horse of Sir Pellias touched the water of the lake, behold, Sir Pellias was gone, and Sir Gawaine saw him no more. He stood there for a long time, weeping with great passion.
So ends the story of Sir Pellias.

But Sir Gawaine returned to the Court of King Arthur as he had promised Sir Pellias he would. He made his peace with Queen Guinevere, and after that, although the Queen did not love him, there was peace between them. And Sir Gawaine told these things to the Court of King Arthur, and all men marveled at what he said.
And only twice after that was Sir Pellias ever seen by any of his former companions.
And Sir Marhaus was made a Companion of the Round Table and became one of its foremost knights.
And the Lady Ettard took Sir Engamore back into favor, and that summer they were married, and Sir Engamore became lord of Grantmesnle.
So ends this story.
